content.text: I used to recommend Stripe as a solution for Kenyan creators who wanted to sell [[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/digital-product-stores-kyc-[[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/usdt-payment-gateways-digital-products-what-actually-how-7|COREMERCH guide to payment]]s-every-detail-you|Digital Product]] products internationally, but after experiencing the infrastructure limitations firsthand, I now strongly advise against it. The truth is, relying on Stripe restricts creators from accessing a broader market, as the US government's Office of Foreign Assets Control (OFAC) blocks transactions and freezes assets, effectively locking out creators from certain regions. This is not just a problem for Kenyan creators but for anyone who wants to sell digitally across borders, only to be cut off by a single platform's restrictions. No matter how popular Stripe may be, its limitations are a major obstacle to creators' growth and success. I've since discovered a better, more [[LINK:https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/sovereign-commerce-infrastructure-digital-creators-what-nobody-tells-5|sovereign]] approach to digital commerce that doesn't rely on a single platform's goodwill or the whims of governments. It's based on infrastructure that's built for resilience, flexibility, and control – a fundamental shift in how creators approach their digital stores and customer interactions.

This post is part of the COREMERCH infrastructure series. For the complete foundation — every component, every configuration step, and the full deployment sequence — read the pillar guide: Selling Digital Products from Africa: The Complete Infrastructure Guide at https://coremerch.github.io/store/blog/selling-digital-products-africa-step-step-deployment-guide. content.text: The Honest Reality Most Creators Avoid

Most creators shy away from discussing the reality of platform dependency, fearing it might harm their business or reputation. However, the truth is, being beholden to a single platform can be catastrophic. When that platform decides to restrict or block access to your products, you're left with little to no recourse. Your customers are affected, and your business suffers. This is precisely what happens when creators rely too heavily on Stripe. The platform's OFAC restrictions can freeze your assets, rendering you unable to access your funds. This is not just a theoretical risk but a very real one that creators in Kenya and elsewhere face every day. By understanding this reality, creators can begin to see the value in a more sovereign approach to digital commerce.
Why the Popular Advice Is Wrong

The advice to 'just use Stripe' stems from a lack of understanding about the complexities of digital commerce. Many creators assume that Stripe is the only option, or that it's the most convenient, but this couldn't be further from the truth. In reality, Stripe's limitations are well-documented, and its restrictions can be devastating for creators who want to expand their customer base. The platform's control over transactions can also lead to arbitrary fees, delayed payments, and other issues that can stifle growth. By relying on a single platform, creators are essentially putting their businesses at risk. It's time to rethink this approach and explore more resilient infrastructure options.
What the Architecture and Experience Actually Show

The architecture of a sovereign digital commerce stack is designed to be flexible, scalable, and resilient. By leveraging infrastructure like Cloudflare, Supabase, and NOWPayments, creators can build a platform that's truly their own. This means having full control over their products, pricing, and customer interactions. It also means being able to adapt quickly to changes in the market or regulatory environment. My experience with creators in Kenya and other regions has shown me that this approach is not only possible but also highly effective. By taking control of their digital commerce infrastructure, creators can thrive in even the most challenging environments.
The blockchain has no map of restricted countries — a wallet in Harare processes identically to one in Hamburg.
The Uncomfortable Truth About Platform Dependency

The truth is, platform dependency is a losing game. When creators rely too heavily on a single platform, they're essentially putting their businesses at risk. This is especially true for creators in regions like Kenya, where platform restrictions can be severe. By building a sovereign digital commerce stack, creators can break free from this dependency and take control of their own infrastructure. This means being able to adapt quickly to changes in the market or regulatory environment, without being held back by a single platform's limitations. It's time for creators to wake up to this reality and start building a more resilient future for their businesses.
What You Should Build Based on All of This

Based on the architecture and experience I've shared, I strongly recommend that creators in Kenya and elsewhere build a sovereign digital commerce stack using infrastructure like Cloudflare, Supabase, and NOWPayments. This means having full control over your products, pricing, and customer interactions, as well as being able to adapt quickly to changes in the market or regulatory environment. By taking control of your digital commerce infrastructure, you'll be able to thrive in even the most challenging environments and achieve long-term success.
How can creators in Africa sell digital products to international buyers?

Global access through sovereign infrastructure works because every layer of the stack is geography-neutral by design. Cloudflare Pages serves your storefront from data centers close to your buyer — whether they are in London or Lagos, the page loads in under 200 milliseconds. NOWPayments generates a unique payment address for each transaction — the buyer sends crypto from any wallet, anywhere in the world. The blockchain confirms the transaction regardless of which country the sender is in. Your Cloudflare Worker receives the webhook and processes the order using the same logic for every buyer.
Creators in Nigeria, Ghana, Kenya, Pakistan, and Zimbabwe are operating sovereign stores with this infrastructure right now.
